title: Why Ticks Suck
summary: Josh and Chuck explain ticks: why they are arachnids rather than insects, the difference between hard and soft ticks, their body and mouthpart anatomy, the questing behavior, the feeding process (cement-like saliva and anticoagulant), the multi-host life cycle, and the diseases they spread such as Lyme disease and Rocky Mountain spotted fever. They give a public-service guide to checking for and removing ticks with tweezers, debunk home remedies, and suggest prevention. The episode closes with a thank-you segment for listener mail, books, candy, CDs, and postcards.

segments.title: Opening banter and tick anecdotes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about Josh's birthday and ages, then Chuck describes a tick-borne Lyme disease case involving a keyboard player from the Henry Clay People after a stay at his house, and Josh mentions the Komodo dragon tick.

segments.title: Ticks are arachnids, not insects
segments.summary: The hosts explain that ticks are arachnids with eight legs, not insects, and are not spiders, and that there are about 850 species. They divide ticks into hard ticks and soft ticks.

segments.title: Tick body, mouthparts and questing
segments.summary: Ticks share a body, eight legs, eyes in many species, and a capitulum with palps, chelicerae and a barbed hypostome. Hard ticks quest by waiting on grass blades with raised front legs to grab passing hosts. Ticks feed only on blood and can sense carbon dioxide and colors.

segments.title: Feeding, saliva and engorgement
segments.summary: Hard ticks feed for long periods and their bodies expand; female hard ticks can swell greatly and lay as many as eighteen thousand eggs after mating. Ticks secrete a cement-like substance and an anticoagulant in their saliva to stay attached and keep blood flowing.

segments.title: Tick life cycle and host stages
segments.summary: The hosts walk through the tick life cycle from larva with six legs to nymph to adult, each stage needing a blood meal, most ticks being three-host ticks, and ticks that fail to feed being able to survive for a long time without reproducing.

segments.title: Tick-borne diseases
segments.summary: Ticks are described as the top disease vector in the animal world and second only to mosquitoes among human disease vectors. Diseases mentioned include Lyme disease with its bull's eye rash, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, and Queensland tick typhus. Transmission takes about four hours, via saliva or regurgitation.

segments.title: Checking for and removing ticks
segments.summary: Advice to check the scalp, armpits, neck, waistband and other dark damp areas every couple of hours. Hosts debunk home remedies such as nail polish, matches, and alcohol, and explain removing a tick with fine tweezers grasped close to the skin, pulled straight up slowly, then washing the area; dropping it in alcohol and bleach is mentioned.

segments.title: Tick prevention and yard care
segments.summary: Prevention tips include light-colored clothing, lint rollers, long sleeves, tucking pants into socks, hats, gloves, insect repellent with DEET, keeping lawns mowed, and dragging a white cloth across the yard to test for ticks. Josh shares a flea infestation story from Los Angeles.

segments.title: Thank-you segment: books, candy and mail
segments.summary: The hosts thank listeners and authors for books including Chuck Norris Cannot Be Stopped, How to Speak Pirate, Revolutions for Fun and Profit, Molecular Gastronomy, The Catcher's Companion, and The Zombie Combat Manual, plus candy from Little Bit of Sweets, hot sauce, CDs, postcards, and beer.
